doc.title: Bill Crow interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, October 18, 1995

title: Writing for Down Beat and the Jazz Review
summary: His first writing came through Nat Hentoff and Down Beat, then musician reviews for the Jazz Review, which he came to dislike.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Critics, polls and the jazz press

blocks.x: Well that’s great. That’s some major scuffling. When did you first start to do some writing?

Well I had done writing just as a writing exercise all through school and college. One of the best college courses I ever took was a creative writing class where the woman gave us a lot of freedom, just showed us how to research and gave us a lot of freedom to write whatever we wanted. And somewhere I think after I started working for Stan Getz in about 1953, in there someplace, I had been through let’s see, Teddy Charles I think was my first really jazz group. I worked with his trio and he taught me all the Bebop changes. And then Jimmy Raney, I came to work with him with Stan Getz wasn’t working, he had been Stan’s regular guitar player, and he took me on to Stan’s band. And right around that time I met a couple of writers for Down Beat, Nat Hentoff I think was still living in Boston and had started writing for Down Beat. And just in chatting with these guys, they realized that I could express myself clearly when talking about music so they would come and ask me what I thought about different things. And eventually somebody asked me to do an article for Down Beat and I did that. And then years later when I think I was with Gerry Mulligan by then, Nat Hentoff and Martin Williams and a guy named Hsio Wen Shih, a Chinese man, started a magazine called the Jazz Review. It only lasted a couple of years. But their idea was to get musicians to write reviews. They thought they could get it closer to the horse’s mouth. So they asked me and I think the people who agreed to write reviews were me, Cannonball Adderley, Bill Evans, gee I can’t remember now. They had quite a stable of guys. They didn’t pay you anything, they’d just give you the records and you would, that way our opinions remained “pure” I believe. But it was a good exercise. It made me really think what I thought about the music and try to say it clearly. I finally decided I didn’t like writing music reviews because there was really a conflict of interest as a professional, you know that even if you used the most careful terms, you could be wounding a colleague’s career, and I just got uncomfortable with it just about the time that the magazine died. I still do occasional book reviews for the union paper whenever they need somebody to do that once in a while. And I don’t really consider myself a © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-
professional writer and I’m not going to get in anybody’s way by saying what I think about some things that I review there, but I don’t really like reviewing music anymore.
What, this was what year about?
The Jazz Review? That was in the 50s, you know I’ve lost track of that completely. Late 50s, early 60s I would imagine.
